title: Introduction to Cloud Computing
learningGoals: Define cloud computing, pay-as-you-go and the service models (IaaS, PaaS, SaaS).

Explain the technical reasons (performance, elasticity, global distribution, high availability and reliability) and the business reasons (no upfront cost, pay per use, faster time to market, less maintenance) for adopting the cloud.
Explain virtualisation, hypervisors (VMMs), and Type 1 (bare-metal) vs Type 2 (hosted), with the pros and cons of VMs.
Explain static vs dynamic provisioning, multi-tenancy, server consolidation, scalability vs elasticity, and how to measure elasticity.
Explain virtualisation overhead and compare VMs vs containers (Docker, Kubernetes): when to use each, and the Netflix microservices example.
sirStressed: "Not a single day goes by without us using the cloud." Know your everyday examples (UPI, Aadhaar, IRCTC Tatkal, Hotstar).
Both technical and business reasons: "without monetary benefits nobody adopts the cloud." Pay-as-you-go, no upfront cost.
Type 1 (bare-metal, data centres, faster, more secure) vs Type 2 (hosted, local development, slower).
Multi-tenancy (Netflix and Airbnb on AWS, logically isolated). Static vs dynamic provisioning. Server consolidation.
Scalability vs elasticity: elasticity is automatic, up and down. Measure it by scaling time, utilisation %, and cost efficiency.

VMs vs containers: isolation (OS vs process), size, startup (minutes vs seconds). "We cannot replace VMs with containers." Containers are for microservices; VMs are for security, legacy and different OSes.
commonTraps: Type 1 runs on the hardware; Type 2 runs on a host OS. VirtualBox is Type 2.
Elasticity ≠ scalability. Elasticity is automatic and goes both ways.
Containers don't include an OS. They share the host kernel, so you can't run a Windows container on a Linux kernel.
Multi-tenancy means shared resources with logical isolation, not shared data.
Docker creates and runs containers; Kubernetes orchestrates many of them.
Server consolidation = fewer servers for low-load apps, not more.
The SaaS, PaaS and IaaS levels of control are often mixed up: IaaS gives the most control; SaaS gives the least.
summary: Cloud = on-demand compute, storage, networking and software over the internet, pay-as-you-go. Models: IaaS (VMs), PaaS (platform), SaaS (apps). Everyday examples: WhatsApp, Gmail, UPI, Aadhaar, IRCTC, Hotstar.
Technical needs: performance, elasticity, global distribution (low latency), high availability (redundancy, auto-failover, disaster recovery).
Business needs: no upfront cost, pay per use, less maintenance, faster time to market, scale without losing customers.

Virtualisation: software computers on shared hardware. Hypervisor/VMM. Type 1 bare-metal (ESXi, Hyper-V, Xen; data centres; fast; secure; complex) vs Type 2 hosted (VirtualBox, VMware Workstation; development and learning; slower).
VM pros: cost, isolation, full OS control, different OSes, migration. Cons: full OS each, overhead, slow boot.
Provisioning: static (fixed) vs dynamic (by load, auto-scaling). Multi-tenancy (Netflix and Airbnb on AWS). Consolidation (low-use apps on one VM).
Scalability (the ability to grow, may be manual) vs elasticity (automatic up and down, pay only for the spike). Measured by scaling time, utilisation %, cost efficiency.

Containers: app + libraries, shared kernel, Docker (create and run) and Kubernetes (orchestrate). Start in seconds, MB-sized, high density, process-level isolation, same-OS only. VMs: minutes, GBs, OS-level isolation, any OS. Use containers for microservices (Netflix); VMs for banking, ERP, legacy and mixed OSes. Containers don't replace VMs.

questions.prompt: Give two technical and two business reasons for a start-up to use the cloud instead of its own servers.
correctAnswers: Technical: elasticity (auto-scale for spikes), global distribution (low latency), high availability and failover, and access to heavy compute such as GPUs. Business: no upfront hardware cost (pay-as-you-go), less maintenance and staff, and faster time to market (live in minutes).

Business: no upfront hardware cost (pay-as-you-go), less maintenance and staff, and faster time to market (live in minutes).

questions.prompt: Distinguish scalability from elasticity, and name the three parameters used to measure elasticity.
correctAnswers: Scalability = the system's ability to grow capacity for more load, which can be manual or planned (adding servers). Elasticity = automatic, dynamic scaling up and down with demand in real time, so you pay only for what you use. Elasticity is measured by scaling time (up or down), resource utilisation %, and cost efficiency.

questions.prompt: A bank must run a legacy core-banking application that needs a specific Windows Server version with strict isolation. It also wants to launch a new mobile-app back end made of 20 microservices that must scale within seconds. Recommend VMs or containers for each, and justify your choice.
correctAnswers: Legacy core banking → VMs. They need a specific OS (Windows Server), strong OS-level isolation and security, and they're legacy. A container can't provide a different OS and gives only process-level isolation. Microservices back end → containers (Docker, orchestrated by Kubernetes, typically on cloud VMs). They're lightweight, start in seconds, scale out quickly, package each service with its dependencies, and give high density. That's the Netflix-style microservices pattern.

questions.prompt: What is server consolidation, and why does it save cost? How is it different from multi-tenancy?
correctAnswers: Server consolidation = putting several low-usage applications onto one (powerful) VM or server instead of giving each its own, which raises utilisation and cuts hardware, power and licence costs. Multi-tenancy = many different customers (tenants) sharing the same infrastructure with logical isolation (Netflix and Airbnb on AWS). Consolidation is about packing workloads efficiently; multi-tenancy is about sharing infrastructure between separate users.
